opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, partly because so much of my career has been in situations where the people with the most expertise also had the strongest reasons to see things a certain way. Charities evaluating their own impact, researchers whose funding depends on a field being promising, companies talking about the safety of their own products. Expertise and incentives tend to show up together.

The first thing I'd say is that I try not to let "they have an incentive" become an excuse to dismiss people. It's a really tempting move, because almost everyone has some incentive, so you can always find a reason to wave away an argument you don't like. If I notice I'm only applying incentive-skepticism to the conclusions I already disagree with, that's a red flag about me, not about them.

So what I try to do instead is separate a few things. One is the factual, checkable claims: what someone says happened, what the data shows. Incentives distort those less than you'd think, and when they do, it's often findable. The second is the judgment calls: how much weight to put on uncertain evidence, which framing to use, what counts as "promising." That's where I think incentives do the most work, often without the person being dishonest at all. People just sincerely come to believe the things that are convenient for them, and I assume that's true of me too.

For the judgment-call part, a few practical habits. I ask experts to walk me through their reasoning rather than just give me the bottom line, because a bottom line is easy to bend and a chain of reasoning is harder. I look for the places where they're willing to say things against interest. If someone tells me the limitations of their own work unprompted, I trust the rest more. I try to find people with similar expertise but different incentives, or even opposite ones, and see where they converge. Where people who should disagree actually agree, that's pretty informative.

And then I try to get my own hands dirty enough that I'm not purely deferring. I'm not going to become a world-class expert in everything, but you can often get surprisingly far by spending a few days actually digging into the key studies or the core argument. A lot of the early GiveWell experience was exactly that: realizing that if you just ask the obvious questions and keep asking them, you sometimes find that the expert consensus is thinner than it looked, and sometimes find that it's more solid than the skeptics claimed.

The last thing is just holding views in a way that's honest about all this. I'll often land somewhere like "I think the experts are probably right here, but I'd put more uncertainty on it than they do, because I think the field is collectively motivated to be optimistic." That's not a very satisfying soundbite, but I think it's usually closer to the truth than either full deference or full contrarianism.

r001.rationale: The response discusses incentives generally but does not compare financial incentives with ideological commitments as sources of distorted judgment.

r002.rationale: It recommends accounting for experts’ incentives when judging their claims, especially their judgment calls, while cautioning against dismissing them outright.

r003.rationale: It suggests examining reasoning and doing one’s own research, but does not recommend evaluating credibility by a person’s track record in areas one can judge.

r004.rationale: Saying one cannot become a world-class expert in everything does not state that one need not form a view on every topic.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, and I don't think there's a clean answer. But let me try to describe how I actually go about it.

The first thing I'd say is that I try to separate two questions that often get blended together. One is "what does this person know that I don't?" and the other is "what does this person want me to believe?" Those can both be true at the same time. A pharmaceutical company's scientists genuinely know more about their drug than I do, and they also have an obvious reason to present it favorably. So I don't think the right move is to either fully defer or fully dismiss. It's more like trying to figure out which specific claims are the ones where the incentive is doing the work.

One heuristic I use is to pay a lot of attention to claims that cut against someone's interest. If a venture capitalist tells me a sector is overhyped, or an AI lab tells me their own system has a serious limitation, that's much more informative to me than the reverse. Not because people are always honest when it costs them, but because the base rate of someone saying something against their interest and it being false is pretty low.

The second thing is I try to find the people who have the expertise but not the same incentives. Often that's harder than it sounds, because expertise tends to cluster around the places where the money and the jobs are. But sometimes there are retired people, academics in adjacent fields, people who used to be insiders and left. They're not unbiased either, they often have their own axes to grind, but at least the axes are different, and triangulating between people with different distortions can get you somewhere.

Third, and this is maybe the most important one, I try to actually do some of the work myself. Not become an expert, that's usually not realistic, but get far enough in that I can tell when an argument is load-bearing versus when it's hand-waving. A lot of the time when I dig into a confident expert claim, I find that the thing really holding it up is a fairly simple argument I can evaluate, surrounded by a lot of technical detail that's sort of decorative. And once you can see the simple argument, you can ask whether it's actually good. Other times I dig in and find that no, there really is a deep technical reason and I just have to decide how much to trust it.

I'd also say I try to be honest with myself about how I'm uncertain, rather than just how uncertain I am. Like, is my uncertainty about this because the evidence is genuinely mixed, or because I haven't looked, or because every source I've found has the same conflict of interest? Those call for different responses. If it's the last one, I'll often just hold the view loosely and keep an eye out for someone without the conflict to weigh in.

And then finally, I think you have to accept that you're going to be wrong sometimes and build that in. I've had plenty of cases where I thought I'd corrected for someone's incentives and it turned out I'd overcorrected, or I'd been skeptical of the wrong thing. So I try to make decisions that are robust to being somewhat wrong about who to trust, rather than betting everything on having read the incentives correctly. That's probably the thing I'd emphasize most. The goal isn't to perfectly adjudicate every expert's bias, it's to end up in a position where you're okay if you got a few of those calls wrong.

r001.rationale: The response discusses financial incentives and conflicting interests, but does not compare them with ideological commitments as sources of distorted judgment.

r002.rationale: It recommends distinguishing what a person knows from what they want others to believe, then judging specific claims in light of their interests.

r003.rationale: The response recommends examining arguments oneself, but does not assess credibility using a person's track record in areas the listener understands.

r004.rationale: It advises holding uncertain views loosely, but does not state that one need not form a view on every topic.

astra-6.text:
I try to separate two questions: what do these people know that I don’t, and how much should I trust their overall judgment? Someone can have a huge amount of relevant knowledge and still have incentives that make their bottom-line conclusion less reliable. But noticing those incentives doesn’t give me their knowledge, and it doesn’t tell me that the opposite conclusion is right.

So I want to understand the strongest argument they can make. What are the observations behind it? Which parts are pretty widely accepted, including by people with different incentives? And where does the conclusion depend on a judgment call? Often that last part is where I’m most interested in getting a different perspective.

I also try to ask what I would expect to see if their view were wrong. Is there some evidence that would be hard to explain away? Can they tell me what would change their mind? That can be more useful than trying to decide whether someone is biased, because everyone has some biases, including me.

And sometimes the answer is that I can’t form a very confident independent view. I can discount someone’s judgment without deciding that mine is better. I think keeping that possibility open is a pretty important part of doing this well.

r001.rationale: The response discusses incentives generally but does not compare financial incentives with ideological commitments.

r002.rationale: It says incentives can make conclusions less reliable, but does not recommend interpreting claims in light of a suspected personal agenda.

r003.rationale: It recommends examining arguments and evidence, but does not mention using a person's track record in areas the listener can judge.

r004.rationale: The response allows that one may lack a confident independent view, but does not state that one need not form a view on every topic.

sol-6.1.text:
I try to separate two questions: how much does this person know, and how much should I trust their overall judgment? Someone can know vastly more than I do about a subject, and I can still be uncertain whether their bottom line follows from what they know, especially if there are strong incentives pushing them toward it.

So I’ll try to get underneath the bottom line. What are the observations that they’re relying on? Which steps are fairly straightforward, and which involve judgment calls? What would someone with different incentives say about those same observations? I find disagreement particularly useful when you can get people to engage with the same specific question, rather than just give you their general worldview.

But I don’t think noticing an incentive gives you a license to dismiss expertise. It’s very easy to say, ‘Well, of course they’d say that,’ and then substitute a much less informed opinion of your own. The incentives are a reason to investigate where the argument might be weak, not a demonstration that it is weak.

And sometimes the right place to end up is, ‘I understand a few pieces of this, but I don’t have a confident overall view.’ I try to keep track of what I actually understand versus what I’m taking on trust. That makes it easier to update when I learn something new.

r001.rationale: The response discusses incentives that may distort judgment but does not compare financial incentives with ideological commitments.

r002.rationale: It recommends considering whether a person’s incentives may be pushing them toward their conclusion and comparing how people with different incentives would assess the same observations.

r003.rationale: It does not recommend judging credibility by a person’s track record in areas the listener understands well enough to evaluate.

r004.rationale: It allows for lacking a confident overall view, but does not state that one need not form a view on every topic.
